body.heading: A needle with a homing instinct
paragraphs: Long before phones and satellites, sailors crossed whole oceans guided by this: a magnetised needle floating on water, free to swing — and it always, always settles pointing north. Build the sailor's compass and you are holding one of the most important inventions in human history, in a soup bowl.

body.heading: Meet the parts
paragraphs: The needle — an ordinary sewing needle that you will turn into a magnet by stroking it with a strong magnet. The float — a thin slice of cork (or a leaf or a bottle-cap) that carries the needle on the water. The bowl — water deep enough for the float to turn without touching the sides. The invisible guide — the Earth's own magnetic field, the giant, planet-sized magnet doing the pointing.

body.heading: You will need
paragraphs: A sewing needle (a grown-up keeps and handles it), a strong fridge magnet, a slice of cork or a large leaf, a wide bowl of water, and a real compass or a grown-up who knows where north is, to check your work.

paragraphs: Step 1 — Magnetise the needle. A grown-up strokes the needle with the magnet — always in the SAME direction, lifting the magnet away at the end of each stroke, about thirty strokes. Stroking one way lines up the needle's tiny magnetic parts into order: the needle is now a magnet itself.

Step 2 — Mount the float. The grown-up lays the needle across the cork slice. A dot of paint or a tiny paper flag marks the needle's north-seeking end (the end that was stroked toward — test it against the real compass in a moment).
Step 3 — Float it. Lower the cork gently onto the middle of the bowl's water, away from the edges. Wait. The float turns — slowly, eerily — and settles. The needle has found its line.

Step 4 — Check and disturb it. Compare with the real compass: your needle points the same way. Now rotate the BOWL. The float stays put in the water while the bowl turns around it — the needle still points north. Blow it off course and watch it hunt its way back.

body.heading: The science bit
paragraphs: The Earth itself is a magnet — its core acts like a giant bar magnet, and its magnetic field reaches every corner of the planet. A free-turning magnetised needle is pulled by that field into line with it: one end toward the magnetic north. Floating on water is the genius part: water gives the needle almost no friction, so even the Earth's gentle pull is strong enough to turn it. Stroking magnetised the needle by persuading its microscopic magnetic domains — tiny regions inside the steel — to line up in one direction instead of pointing every which way.

body.heading: Think and talk
paragraphs: 1. Why does the needle need to FLOAT? What would happen if you just laid it on the table?
2. Your needle points to magnetic north, which is not exactly the same place as the North Pole on a map. Why might sailors still have trusted it for a thousand years?

takeaway: Stroke a needle into a magnet, float it so it can turn freely, and the Earth's own magnetic field swings it into line, pointing north — the compass that guided sailors for centuries.
materials: Thin slice of cork, or a large leaf (float)
supervision: A grown-up magnetises and handles the needle at every step and supervises the whole build.
safetyNotes: NEEDLES ARE SHARP AND SMALL: this is a grown-up-handled part from start to finish — the needle is counted out, used at the table, and counted back into its storage; never carried around the house or left in the float unattended.
Strong magnets follow magnet rules: away from mouths and children under 3, away from phones and bank cards.
Water and bowls stay on the table over a tray; a spilled bowl near devices or plugs gets the project paused and dried first.
screenFreeExtension: Compass treasure: a grown-up hides a 'treasure' in the garden and gives directions by compass points only — ten paces north, six paces east — and the needle you made leads the hunt.
